title: What the Deep Keeps
passages:
She wrote the names on the back of her glove first, in grease pencil, hard enough to score the vinyl. SOL. DEY. NIA. TEO. SALAS. WREN. Then she hung her spare slate on a nail at the ward door where the light could find it, because a slate she wasn't wearing couldn't be edited, and she had stopped being sure that was a rule anybody else agreed with.
"Forty-two and a hair," she said. "Going off the good air."
"Copy forty-two," Nia said, pencil already going. "Dey's at six breaths. The pauses are longer."
"Write the pauses down. Don't round them."
Sol's voice came over the top of the pencil, with the ratchet knocking behind it. "Forty-one turns. The counter glass is fogged, I'm counting by hand, so nobody talk to me for a minute. Wren — every ten meters, out loud."
Her suit was a rebreather, which meant it scrubbed the carbon dioxide out of what she breathed out and handed the rest back for another go; below forty-two the scrubber canister stopped being rated, and she went onto bailout — open circuit, one breath in, one breath straight out into the water, nothing kept. No spare bottle. The gauge said nine minutes and it was not a generous gauge.
The stairwell went down in a flooded square, four flights to a landing, a wheelchair parked on the third with its footplates folded like it had manners. Tiles, then ceiling, then tiles.
"Forty-five." A swell came through the blown window on the east side, hit the far wall, and the tower leaned and came back. The corridor along the landing shut by a hand's width. She put her palm flat on the tile to be sure she hadn't imagined it. "Walls are walking. One hand a swell. Log it."
"Logged."
At forty-six she stopped, because a name had gone out of her. All six were still on the glove. Five of them were people. The second one was letters in a row.
"Copy, Wren?"
"Copy. Moving."
At forty-nine the stairwell let out into the dispensary, and the cases weren't in the dispensary. They were out on the landing floor, side by side, squared up, latches facing the stairs the way you set a load you mean to carry. The tile had gouges in it from the corners. Somebody had walked them out through a door that opened inward against a fallen shelf, and it had taken a while, and that somebody had had more air than she had now.
They were lashed. Orange twine, three turns and a tuck, tail long, pulled down hard on the handles. She had tied that knot at the pocket. She tied it in her sleep. She had never in her life tied a knot she couldn't read afterwards, and she read this one twice.
"Sol. The cases are already rigged."
A pause with iron in it. "By who."
"By me." Her voice came out wrong inside the helmet. "There's an hour down here I don't have. I was on this landing. I did the work, I came back up, and it's gone—"
"Come up," Sol said. "Come up now, we'll take the tower on the drum and try again—"
"There's forty-nine meters of building between me and air and a gap behind me the width of my shoulders." Her gauge had gone a step further than it should have. "Hang on."
Behind her, up the corridor at forty-two, the pocket went. Not a sound so much as a shove: the last of the air came out of the ceiling in one silver rush, past her lamp, up the stairwell and gone, and Ivo Salas came out with it, still on his twine, both hands loose off the rail, drifting down into the corridor at the head of the stairs.
No room now. No air up there at all.
And the twine in her fist went tight, took up its slack, and started to rise — hand over hand, patient, the way a man pulls himself along a line when he has decided where he is going and does not have the breath to say so.

The twine sang in her glove, a thin keen under the regulator's roar. She fed it out hand over hand, not fighting — fighting spent gas she didn't have — and watched the dark resolve into a shape pulling itself toward her, one arm, pause, the other arm, pause, the helmet lamps painting the corridor in twin cones that trembled with each swell.

Salas reached the landing and did not stop. His boots skidded on the gouged tile, momentum carrying him past the cases, past her, until the twine ran out and snapped him back like a dog on a lead. He hung there, suspended in the stairwell's mouth, chest barely moving.

"Salas." She grabbed his harness D-ring, hauled him upright. "Salas, look at me."

His eyes opened. The pupils were wide, fixed. Carbon dioxide does that — steals the reflex before it steals the consciousness.

"Four-nine," she said. "Dispensary landing. Cases are rigged. You're going up on the main cable."

No answer. His lips moved, soundless.

She drew her knife — the small serrated one on her chest strap, not the heavy line cutter at her hip — and sawed through the orange twine where it vanished into his harness. The cut end whipped away, gone up the stairwell. He was free of the ward rail. Free of the pocket. Just her and the ascent cable now.

The cable ran down the stairwell's center, thick as her wrist, streaked with rust and something darker. She clipped his chest D-ring to it with a locking carabiner, then took the standing part and began the knot. Three turns around the cable, tight as she could make them with gloves numb from cold and pressure. Tuck the tail. Pull the standing part. Dress it. Set it. Tail long, hanging like a signature.

"Three turns and a tuck," she said aloud, for Nia. "Tail long. Salas on the cable."

His breathing hitched. Four shallow gasps in a minute, maybe five. The bubbles from his exhaust valve came slow, each one smaller than the last.

Her gauge flashed: *four minutes*. Not nine. Four.

"Nia," she keyed. "Salas rigged. Four gasps a minute. Cases still on the landing."

"Logged," Nia said. The pencil scratched. "Dey's at four. Pauses twenty seconds."

Wren didn't let herself think about Dey. She unclipped her own tether from the landing's rusted rail, clipped it to the cable above Salas, and turned toward the medicine cases sitting squared up on the gouged tile — latches facing the stairs, orange twine frosted with pressure ice, waiting for her hands.

The gauge read *04:00* when she set the knife to the carrying lash.

The orange twine had gone stiff as wire in the cold. The serrations took it in three drags and one swear word, and the case came off the tile into her arms with no manners at all — sealed, dry, and a hard negative in the water, forty kilos of pharmacy with no intention of floating and none whatever of being carried by one cold woman with four minutes of gas.

She braced it against the cable with her knee and got line out of her thigh pouch. Six millimeter. No cable clamps; she didn't own cable clamps. What she had was a rolling hitch, which bites harder the more the load pulls and lets go if you tap the tail back the other way. Six turns up the cable from the low side, worked so the weight seats the knot instead of stripping it.

*03:35.*

Her gloves had gone stupid. She read the back of the left one between turns: SOL. DEY. NIA. TEO. SALAS. WREN. Five people and a row of letters, and her hands went on working anyway, because her hands were the part of her that had stood on this landing before and remembered the job.

Carabiner through the case handle, gate screwed down. Second case above the first, cross-lashed so the two rode as one lump — two lumps on one line swing, and a swinging lump at forty meters is how you find a wall.

*03:10.*

All of it above Salas. If the drum gave her slack, she wanted the crates going up and away, not down onto a man with four gasps in him.

"Salas." Palm flat on his helmet, tipping his lamp up. "You're under the load. Stay under it."

His lips moved. No bubbles came with it.

Four latches, two to a case, cam latches, the kind you shut with your heel. She thumbed every one and felt every cam seat. *02:40.* Then the seal wire on the near case — turned it until the lead crimp showed in her lamp, unbroken, the Factor's little stamp still legible. Whatever the Factor wanted was still in there. Teo's course was still in there, or enough of it, and she was not going to do that arithmetic with two minutes on her chest.

Then the stairwell, because the load rode wide. Cases an arm's length above her helmet, two hands outboard of the cable, and the inside corner came in at the second flight. She put her lamp on the gap and waited out a swell while the tower leaned and came back.

*02:05.*

The corner stopped a hand's width short of the case ends. She put her glove into the gap to be sure of it, took it out again, and did not like how few hands that was.

"Nia. Tell Sol the load's wide — two cases, one arm up, two hands out. Clears at forty-two. At forty it's close."

"Close how close?"

"Close as one swell."

"I'll tell her."

"Tell her now."

Dey's numbers came up under Nia's pencil: four breaths, pause at twenty seconds, pause at twenty-two.

Sol came over the top of all of it, ratchet knocking. "Wren. Spliced line at forty, no brake on this drum, one hand. When you're rigged you say go and I go, and after that I'm not talking to you either."

*01:35.*

Wren got her left arm through the bight of the cable, her right glove on the standing part above her head, and her boots planted on either side of Salas's shoulders — the load over her, the man under her, and her in the middle of the only two things down here worth four minutes of anybody's air.

She keyed the mic with her chin.

"Go," she said. "Bring us up."

The cable came tight. Somewhere above, iron took up the strain, the cases swung out over the gouged tile, and behind her the corner of the second flight ground once against nothing.

The drum took the strain like a held breath. Sol's boots were welded to the deck plate, knees locked, the ratchet handle braced against her hip the way she'd braced it a thousand times — left hand on the drum flange feeling for the splice, right hand driving the handle down and up, down and up, each stroke a half-turn she counted in her throat because the counter glass had fogged solid an hour ago and nobody had the rag to clear it.

"Forty-two turns," she muttered. "Forty-three. Forty-four — *shit*."

The splice hit the fairlead hard. Not a whisper, not a rub — a *clunk* that traveled up the drum shaft into her wrist bones, the hand-spliced section swelling past the roller's throat because somebody had served it too thick or the storm had swollen the fibers or the sea just decided today was the day. The drum kept turning. The fairlead didn't. The line piled up in a loose coil beside the roller, slack blooming between drum and lead, and the weight below — two cases, one man, one woman — stopped rising.

"Sol." Nia's voice, thin over the wind. "The load's stopped. Forty meters on the nose."

"I can see the turns, Nia." She didn't look up. Couldn't. The coil was growing, a snake of wet Dyneema eating deck space, and if it kinked under the next stroke she'd lose the lot — cable, cases, people, the whole bloody afternoon. No brake on this drum. Never had one. The ratchet pawl only caught one way, and the load was pulling *out*.

She let go of the handle.

The drum spun free.

The sound was a scream — metal on metal, the pawl skipping teeth, the handle whipping past her ear close enough to taste grease. The coil vanished over the gunwale in a single hungry rush. The Marrow heeled hard to starboard as a swell took her broadside, the deck canting until Sol's boots slid on the nonskid, and the line ran out into the dark with the storm's full weight behind it, ten seconds of pure gravity and no hand on the wheel.

*One. Two. Three.*

She threw herself at the flange, fingers finding the spinning drum's edge, skin burning as she rode the rotation — not stopping it, never stopping it, just *guiding* the rope back into the fairlead's throat with her palm while the drum howled and the pawl chattered like a machine gun.

*Four. Five. Six.*

The splice fought her. Thick, stubborn, the served section refusing the roller's curve until she got her thumbnail into the lay and *persuaded* it, one fiber at a time, the salt and pressure ice grinding under her nail.

*Seven. Eight.*

The load came back alive. She felt it in the drum — a sudden heavy pulse, the cases and the man and the woman biting down again, the line singing tight from fairlead to water. The drum slowed. The pawl caught. The handle settled against her hip, waiting.

*Nine. Ten.*

Sol exhaled. Her left hand was raw, the thumbnail torn to the quick, and the ratchet handle was warm where her palm had stayed welded through the free run. The counter glass was still fogged. She had no idea how many turns she'd lost, how many she'd gained, whether the math still worked for forty-nine meters and a safety margin.

"Load's moving," she said. Her voice sounded like somebody else's. "Forty-five turns. Maybe forty-six. Nia — log *maybe*."

"Logged. Dey's at three breaths. Pause twenty-four seconds."

The splice passed the fairlead clean on the next revolution, and the one after, and the one after that — smooth now, the served section bedded in, the drum eating line in steady half-turns while the Marrow shuddered under a wave that broke green over the bow. Sol drove the handle down. Up. Down. Up. The wind screamed through the rigging like a thing with teeth, and somewhere below the water the load was either rising or it wasn't, and Dey on deck was at three breaths with twenty-four seconds between them, and the only number she could trust was the one burning in her thumb.
